Constantine
KON-stan-teen
proper noun (Roman emperor, c. 272–337)
Latin Constantinus, from constans (“steadfast, constant”); the Roman emperor (reigned 306–337) who ended the persecution of Christians and summoned the Council of Nicaea.

📖 Biblical Definition

Constantine was the Roman emperor whose reign marked the great turning of the empire from the persecution of the church toward its favour. The dictionary marks two acts of lasting weight. By the Edict of Milan in 313, Constantine and his co-emperor granted toleration to the Christians, ending the bloody persecutions under which the saints had suffered for nearly three centuries and giving the church liberty to worship openly. And in 325 he summoned and presided over the first ecumenical council, the Council of Nicaea, which against the Arian denial of the Son's deity confessed Christ to be of one substance with the Father, very God of very God. The dictionary honours God's providence in both. The same Lord who turneth the king's heart whithersoever He will, and in whose hand are the kings of the earth, used this emperor to stay the sword from His people and to gather the bishops who guarded the deity of His Son. The dictionary gives thanks for the rest granted the church and for the orthodoxy Nicaea confessed. Yet it names plainly the perils that followed the marriage of church and state begun under Constantine. The favour of emperors brought wealth, power, and worldliness into the church; soon the state would meddle in doctrine, persecute dissenters, and bend the church to imperial ends, and the seeds were sown of a Christendom in which the kingdom of Christ was confounded with the kingdoms of this world. Our Lord's kingdom is not of this world, and the church's weapons are not carnal but mighty through God. The dictionary therefore honours Constantine's providential acts—the peace and the council—while warning that the embrace of Caesar has ever been a more subtle danger to the church's purity than the sword of Caesar.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Roman emperor (c. 272–337) who ended persecution by the Edict of Milan (313) and summoned the Council of Nicaea (325); honoured for God's providence in both, with the perils of the church-state entanglement that followed named.

CONSTANTINE, proper noun. [Latin constans, steadfast.] The Roman emperor (reigned 306–337).

By the Edict of Milan (313) he ended the persecution of Christians.

He summoned and presided over the Council of Nicaea (325).

Nicaea confessed Christ of one substance with the Father against Arius.

Honoured in providence, with the perils of church-state entanglement named.

📖 Key Scripture

Pr 21:1 — "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."

Da 2:21 — "And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:"

Joh 18:36 — "Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence."

2 Co 10:4 — "(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The marriage of church and state begun under Constantine brought wealth, worldliness, and imperial meddling into the church, sowing the seeds of a Christendom that confounded Christ's kingdom with the kingdoms of this world.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary first honours God's providence in Constantine's reign. The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, who turneth it whithersoever He will; by this emperor God ended through the Edict of Milan the long and bloody persecutions under which His saints had suffered, and gave the church liberty to worship openly. And through the Council of Nicaea, which Constantine summoned, God gathered the bishops who confessed His Son to be of one substance with the Father, very God of very God, against the Arian denial. For the rest granted His people and the orthodoxy guarded at Nicaea, the dictionary gives genuine thanks.

Yet the perils that followed must be named. The favour of emperors brought wealth, power, and worldliness into a church that had been purified by suffering; the state soon meddled in doctrine, exiled and persecuted dissenters in the name of Christ, and bent the church to imperial ends. Here were sown the seeds of a Christendom in which the kingdom of the crucified was confounded with the kingdoms of this world. But our Lord said plainly, My kingdom is not of this world, and the weapons of the church's warfare are not carnal but mighty through God. The dictionary honours the providential acts—the peace and the council—while warning that the embrace of Caesar has ever proved a subtler danger to the church's purity than the sword of Caesar, and that the church flourishes by the Word and the Spirit, not by the patronage of princes.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin constans (“steadfast”); the emperor Constantine, whose Edict of Milan and Council of Nicaea turned the empire from persecuting to favouring the church.

Roman emperor, reigned 306–337.
